title: 06 — Apache Spark
html:
06 — Apache Spark

The one idea: Spark splits data into partitions, ships your code to where each partition is, and runs it in parallel. Everything is cheap until data has to move between machines — the shuffle. Understanding Spark performance is mostly understanding when and why a shuffle happens, and how big and even its partitions are.

1. Architecture

---
title: Spark application architecture
---
flowchart TB
    D["Driver<br/>SparkSession, planner,<br/>DAG and task scheduler"]
    CM["Cluster manager<br/>(Databricks, YARN, Kubernetes, standalone)"]
    subgraph W1["Worker node 1"]
        E1["Executor<br/>task slots (cores)<br/>memory + cache"]
    end
    subgraph W2["Worker node 2"]
        E2["Executor<br/>task slots (cores)<br/>memory + cache"]
    end
    subgraph W3["Worker node 3"]
        E3["Executor<br/>task slots (cores)<br/>memory + cache"]
    end
    D <-->|"request resources"| CM
    CM --> W1
    CM --> W2
    CM --> W3
    D -->|"send tasks"| E1
    D -->|"send tasks"| E2
    D -->|"send tasks"| E3
    E1 <-->|"shuffle data"| E2
    E2 <-->|"shuffle data"| E3
    ST[("Cloud storage<br/>ADLS / S3")] <--> E1
    ST <--> E2
    ST <--> E3
Component Role Failure impact
Driver Runs your main program or notebook, holds the SparkSession, turns code into a plan, splits it into stages and tasks, schedules tasks, tracks results Driver dies → the whole application fails
Executors JVM processes on worker nodes that run tasks, each using one core per task slot, and store cached data and shuffle files Executor dies → its tasks are retried elsewhere; lost shuffle output is recomputed
Cluster manager Allocates machines/containers to the application —

Key consequences:

  • Data flows between executors and storage, not through the driver. Calling collect() or toPandas() on a large DataFrame pulls everything into driver memory and is a common way to crash a job.
  • Parallelism = number of task slots (total executor cores). A 10-worker cluster with 8 cores each runs 80 tasks at once.
  • On Databricks, one cluster has one driver node and N worker nodes; typically one executor per worker.

2. RDD vs DataFrame vs Dataset

RDD DataFrame Dataset
Abstraction Distributed collection of objects Distributed table with named, typed columns Typed objects with a schema
Languages Scala, Java, Python All (Python, SQL, Scala, Java, R) Scala, Java only
Optimised by Catalyst No Yes Yes (partially; lambdas are opaque)
Memory format JVM objects (or pickled Python) Compact binary (Tungsten) Compact binary
When to use Rarely: legacy code or very low-level control Almost always Scala teams wanting compile-time types

In PySpark you work with DataFrames and Spark SQL. Both compile to the same plans, so choose by readability: spark.sql("...") and the DataFrame API perform identically.

3. Lazy evaluation: transformations and actions

Transformations describe a new DataFrame (select, filter, join, groupBy().agg(), withColumn). They return immediately and do no work.

Actions ask for a result (count, collect, show, write, toPandas, take). Only an action triggers execution.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = spark.read.table("silver.orders")            # nothing read yet
recent = orders.filter(F.col("order_date") >= "2026-09-01")   # still nothing
by_cust = recent.groupBy("customer_id").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("spend"))  # still nothing

by_cust.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("gold.customer_spend_sept")  # action: runs everything

Why laziness matters: Spark sees the whole pipeline before running it, so the Catalyst optimizer can push the filter into the Parquet/Delta scan, read only customer_id, order_date and amount, and skip files by statistics. You can inspect the plan:

by_cust.explain(mode="formatted")

Pitfall: every action re-runs the plan from the source unless something is cached. Calling df.count() for logging and then df.write executes the pipeline twice.

4. Narrow vs wide transformations

---
title: Narrow vs wide transformations
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph N["Narrow: filter, select, withColumn"]
        NP1["Partition 1"] --> NQ1["Partition 1'"]
        NP2["Partition 2"] --> NQ2["Partition 2'"]
        NP3["Partition 3"] --> NQ3["Partition 3'"]
    end
    subgraph WD["Wide: groupBy, join, distinct"]
        WP1["Partition 1"] --> WQ1["Partition A"]
        WP1 --> WQ2["Partition B"]
        WP2["Partition 2"] --> WQ1
        WP2 --> WQ2
        WP3["Partition 3"] --> WQ1
        WP3 --> WQ2
    end
Narrow (no shuffle) Wide (shuffle)
select, filter/where, withColumn, drop, union, map-style UDFs, coalesce groupBy().agg(), join (non-broadcast), distinct, dropDuplicates, orderBy, repartition, window functions with partitionBy
Each output partition depends on one input partition Each output partition depends on many input partitions
Pipelined together in one stage Creates a stage boundary

5. Jobs, stages, tasks and the DAG

  • Job: all the work triggered by one action.
  • Stage: a set of tasks that can run without a shuffle. Stages are separated by shuffle boundaries (wide transformations).
  • Task: one unit of work on one partition, run on one core.
---
title: One job split into stages at shuffle boundaries
---
flowchart LR
    A["Stage 1<br/>scan orders + filter<br/>200 tasks"] -->|"shuffle by customer_id"| C["Stage 3<br/>join + aggregate<br/>200 tasks"]
    B["Stage 2<br/>scan customers<br/>20 tasks"] -->|"shuffle by customer_id"| C
    C --> D["Write output<br/>files"]

Stage 1 and stage 2 have no dependency on each other and can run concurrently. Stage 3 cannot start until both have written their shuffle output.

The number of tasks in a stage equals the number of partitions it processes:

  • For a file scan: roughly total input size ÷ spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes (default 128 MB).
  • After a shuffle: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (default 200), adjusted at runtime by AQE.

6. Partitions and the shuffle

A partition is the unit of parallelism. Too few partitions → idle cores and huge tasks that spill. Too many → scheduling overhead and tiny output files.

Rule of thumb: target ~100–200 MB per partition after a shuffle, and at least 2–3× as many partitions as total cores.

The shuffle writes each task's output to local disk, bucketed by the target partition, then every downstream task fetches its bucket from every upstream executor over the network. It costs disk I/O, network, serialisation, and memory — which is why reducing shuffle volume is the first lever in tuning.

df.rdd.getNumPartitions()          # how many partitions now

df.repartition(400, "customer_id") # full shuffle into 400 partitions hashed by key
df.coalesce(50)                    # merge down to 50 partitions, no full shuffle

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "auto")  # Databricks: let AQE choose (Databricks-specific value)

Ways to reduce shuffles:

  • Filter and project before joins and aggregations.
  • Broadcast small tables (§7).
  • Aggregate before joining when you only need aggregates.
  • Avoid unnecessary orderBy, distinct and repartition calls.

7. Join strategies

Strategy How it works Shuffle? When Spark picks it
Broadcast hash join Small side is collected and sent to every executor, built into a hash table; big side is streamed through it No shuffle of the big side One side is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB default in open-source Spark; Databricks may use larger/adaptive thresholds), or a broadcast hint is given, or AQE detects a small side at runtime
Sort-merge join Both sides shuffled by key, sorted, then merged Yes, both sides Default for large equi-joins where neither side is small
Shuffle hash join Both sides shuffled; the smaller side of each partition is built into a hash table Yes, both sides When one side is much smaller than the other but too big to broadcast, and preference settings/AQE allow it; avoids the sort
Broadcast nested loop join Broadcast one side and compare every pair No Non-equi joins (a.ts BETWEEN b.start AND b.end) with a small side
Cartesian product Every row with every row Yes Cross joins; almost always a mistake at scale 
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

enriched = orders.join(broadcast(dim_store), "store_id", "left")

SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(s) */ o.*, s.region
FROM silver.orders o
JOIN gold.dim_store s ON o.store_id = s.store_id;

Cautions with broadcast: the small table is collected through the driver and copied to every executor. Broadcasting a 2 GB table can crash the driver or exhaust executor memory. Check the in-memory size, which can be several times the compressed file size.

8. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)

Static plans are built from estimates, and estimates are often wrong after filters and joins. AQE (on by default since Spark 3.2) re-plans at each shuffle boundary using actual statistics:

AQE feature What it fixes
Coalescing shuffle partitions 200 default shuffle partitions but only 50 MB of data → merges into a few right-sized partitions
Switching join strategies A side that turned out small after filtering is broadcast instead of sort-merged
Skew join optimisation Detects partitions much larger than the median and splits them into sub-partitions, replicating the matching side

AQE makes many manual tunings unnecessary, but it cannot fix skew in aggregations as effectively as in joins, cannot fix bad file layout, and only acts at shuffle boundaries.

9. Data skew and salting

Skew means a few keys hold a large share of rows. In the Spark UI it shows as one or a few tasks in a stage running far longer than the median (e.g. median 20 s, max 25 min), often with spill.

Common causes: a dominant customer or country, NULL join keys (all nulls hash to the same partition), default values like 'UNKNOWN' or -1.

Fixes in order of preference:

  1. Filter or separately handle the hot key, e.g. drop NULL keys before an inner join (they can never match anyway).
  2. Let AQE's skew join handling work (check it is enabled and thresholds suit your data).
  3. Broadcast the other side if it is small enough.
  4. Salt the key.

Salting a skewed join: spread the big side's hot key across N sub-keys, and replicate the small side N times.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

N = 16  # salt buckets

big_salted = big.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))

small_salted = (small
    .withColumn("salt", F.explode(F.array([F.lit(i) for i in range(N)]))))

joined = big_salted.join(small_salted, ["customer_id", "salt"]).drop("salt")

Salting a skewed aggregation: aggregate in two phases.

partial = (events
    .withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * 16).cast("int"))
    .groupBy("country", "salt").agg(F.count("*").alias("cnt")))

final = partial.groupBy("country").agg(F.sum("cnt").alias("cnt"))

(For simple sums and counts Spark already does partial aggregation before the shuffle, so salting aggregations mostly helps with non-decomposable operations such as collect_list or exact distinct counts per hot key.)

10. Caching and persistence

from pyspark import StorageLevel
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

features = spark.read.table("silver.events").filter("event_date >= '2026-09-01'")
features.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
features.count()   # materialise the cache

per_user = features.groupBy("user_id").agg(F.count("*").alias("events"))
per_session = features.groupBy("session_id").agg(F.max("event_time").alias("last_seen"))
per_user.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("gold.user_event_counts")
per_session.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("gold.session_last_seen")

features.unpersist()
Cache when Do not cache when
The same DataFrame is reused by several actions It is used once
Recomputing it is expensive (wide joins, complex parsing) Reading it from Delta is already fast (Databricks disk cache helps here automatically)
It fits comfortably in cluster memory It is huge and would evict everything else

Databricks also has a disk cache (formerly "Delta cache") that automatically caches remote Parquet data on workers' local SSDs. It is separate from df.cache() and needs no code.

11. Spill

When a task's data for a sort, aggregation or join does not fit in execution memory, Spark writes intermediate data to local disk and reads it back later. The Spark UI shows Spill (Memory) and Spill (Disk) per stage and task.

Spill is not an error, but heavy spill means slow tasks. Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix
Too few shuffle partitions for the data size Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions or let AQE set it
Skew: one partition far bigger than others See §9
Wide rows (big strings, arrays) Select only needed columns before the shuffle
Executors with too little memory per core Use memory-optimised instance types
explode producing huge row counts Filter before exploding

12. Reading the Spark UI

The Spark UI (in Databricks: cluster → Spark UI, or from a query's execution details) is where performance problems become visible.

Tab What to look at
Jobs Which action is slow; number of stages; failed jobs
Stages Duration, input/output size, shuffle read/write, spill, and the task time distribution (min / median / max). A max far above the median = skew.
SQL / DataFrame The executed physical plan as a graph: join types chosen (BroadcastHashJoin vs SortMergeJoin), rows output per operator, files and bytes read vs pruned, AQE changes
Storage What is cached and how much memory it uses
Executors GC time (high = memory pressure), failed tasks, per-executor shuffle and input
Environment Effective configuration values

A practical triage sequence for a slow job:

  1. Find the longest stage.
  2. Compare max vs median task time → skew?
  3. Check spill → too few partitions or skew?
  4. Check shuffle write size → can you filter, project or broadcast earlier?
  5. In the SQL tab, check files read vs pruned → is data skipping or partition pruning working?
  6. Check for many tiny tasks → small files or too many partitions.

13. PySpark idioms worth knowing

from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

orders = spark.read.table("silver.orders")

# Deduplicate: keep the latest record per key
w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())
latest = (orders
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter("rn = 1")
    .drop("rn"))

# Conditional columns without UDFs
labelled = latest.withColumn(
    "size_band",
    F.when(F.col("amount") >= 1000, "large")
     .when(F.col("amount") >= 100, "medium")
     .otherwise("small"))

# Parse JSON with an explicit schema (no inference cost, stable types)
schema = "event_id STRING, user_id STRING, ts TIMESTAMP, props MAP<STRING, STRING>"
parsed = (spark.read.table("bronze.raw_events")
    .withColumn("e", F.from_json("payload", schema))
    .select("e.*", "_ingested_at"))

# Running total per customer
w2 = (Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("order_date")
      .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))
running = latest.withColumn("running_spend", F.sum("amount").over(w2))

Anti-patterns:

  • Python UDFs for logic that built-in functions can express (they serialise every row to a Python worker).
  • collect() / toPandas() on large data.
  • Loops that build a DataFrame with union hundreds of times (plan explosion); build a list and union once, or restructure.
  • df.count() purely for logging in production jobs.
  • Schema inference on large JSON/CSV at every run.

Azure / .NET mapping

Concept Microsoft stack
Managed Spark Azure Databricks; also Synapse Spark pools and Fabric Spark
Storage for Spark ADLS Gen2 via abfss:// paths, governed through Unity Catalog external locations
.NET and Spark .NET for Apache Spark is no longer actively developed; .NET teams typically use PySpark or SQL for Spark and call Databricks from .NET via the Jobs/SQL REST APIs or the Databricks SQL ODBC/JDBC drivers
Mental model for .NET developers A DataFrame is like an IQueryable: composing it builds an expression tree; the provider (Catalyst) optimises and executes it only when enumerated (an action)

Review checklist

  • I can draw the driver/executor/cluster-manager architecture and say what fails when each dies.
  • I know why DataFrames are preferred over RDDs.
  • I can explain lazy evaluation and why it enables optimisation.
  • I can classify a transformation as narrow or wide.
  • I can explain jobs, stages and tasks, and what determines the number of tasks.
  • I know the join strategies and how to force or avoid a broadcast.
  • I can explain what AQE changes at runtime.
  • I can detect skew in the Spark UI and apply salting.
  • I know when caching helps and when it hurts.
  • I can run the slow-job triage sequence in the Spark UI.
